World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: The long road to recovery after concussion
World.content:
It was 18 months before Liam Dennis could run again without getting headaches.

A keen amateur Port Lincoln footy player, Mr Dennis felt he was at the top of his game when, in 2023, he suffered a serious blow to the head.

"I was, funny enough, being a short-ass in the ruck," he said.

Liam Dennis says it is important to listen to your body when recovering from a concussion. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

"It was a ball up in the pocket and I went up; the other fella went to hit the ball and basically just spiked my head instead of the ball.

"That was the end of footy for me, unfortunately."

There was a long recovery waiting for him, but it was not the first time Mr Dennis had experienced a concussion.

"I've had up to, I think, seven or eight now," he said.

Liam Dennis says he has felt supported by his work and friends throughout his recovery. (Supplied: Rosalie Calderwood)

"I had a lot in junior footy, which I think was probably part of my issue now."

The 27-year-old said recovery after his 2023 knock was rough.

"I'd have a couple of months off work and just extreme fatigue, constant headaches for four months straight … not much fun at that time.

Liam Dennis says his time playing footy came to an end after a serious concussion in 2023. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

"I tried to go back out to the footy after I was a bit better and I still couldn't even hang around in the change rooms with the boys if they were singing the song.

"It was just way too loud and caused this fight-or-flight reaction that I needed to get out and go somewhere quiet."

Feeling 'not normal'

"While his headaches are manageable now, some symptoms have proven difficult to bounce back from.

"The majority of ones that annoy me and give me trouble is like vestibular problems, like balance issues," he said.

" You feel like you're not normal; you know something's not right but you can't really fix it. "

Long-term effects still a mystery

Hunter Bennett, a senior lecturer in exercise science at Adelaide University, said while the short-term impacts of concussions were clear, the long-term implications were not as well known.

"We do see a host of side effects that happen after a concussion," Dr Bennett said.

Hunter Bennett says while researchers have a better understanding of concussions today, the long-term implications are not clear. (BTN High: Cale Matthews)

"These can be things like an inability to focus, sensitivity to light … this can often come with headaches and in some situations, loss of balance.

"It does look like people who have experienced a concussion in the past are going to be more likely to experience a concussion in the future."

Dr Bennett said researchers had a better understanding today of concussion care and rehabilitation compared to 10 years ago.

"But generally, these sorts of recovery processes are best monitored by someone like a physiotherapist or someone who has experience in assessing these neurocognitive factors that can happen after a concussion, because then you can get something that's a little bit more individualised to you."

Attitudes changing, but more education needed

Jeziah Sundqvist says he sees concussions often, both as a physio and footy umpire. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

In Port Lincoln, sports and exercise physiotherapist Jeziah Sundqvist says the conversations around concussions are changing.

"I've been a physio for 20 years. I remember sitting on a bench, removing someone with a concussion [from a football match], having a coach ask them if they were OK to return.

"The player said they were and went back on, and that player didn't have any idea where they were.

"That was a long time ago, but that was the sort of thing that would happen. These days in Port Lincoln, I think there's a much better understanding."

Prior to 2024, the rest period following a concussion was 12 days under SANFL guidelines.

Today, the earliest a player can return to play is on the 21st day after a concussion, following medical clearance.

Jeziah Sundqvist says athletes are becoming more aware of the risks of concussions. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

But it will still take time and education for concussions to be better understood, Mr Sundqvist says.

"I think players themselves are heaps more aware … they're happy to sit out if they don't feel right.

"But it's harder when they feel right and want to go back."

When do you call it quits?

As for when it was time to hang up the boots, Mr Sundqvist said it was a "tricky question".

"The recommendations, and I completely agree with this, is that it needs to be a multi-factorial decision," he said.

Liam Dennis is a keen footy and baseball player, but a series of concussions forced him to step back from sport. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

"Generally, if we look at how it's managed in elite sport, we can still do it to a certain extent here. There might be a player's partner … school teachers, medical practitioners and everybody should all be on the same page about that decision-making process.

"And the athlete themselves, they need to understand that decision that's being made with their involvement.

"But if we think of some of the higher-profile cases that we've seen … Angus Brayshaw quite famously after he Magpies' Maynard cleared by AFL Tribunal , the decision was made that he shouldn't play anymore."

Former Melbourne Demons star Angus Brayshaw was forced into retirement because of concussion issues. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

Mr Dennis said he hoped to see more investment into concussion research in the near future, and that it was important to listen to your body.

"I kept pushing it thinking, 'no, I'm tougher than this, I'm not going to let it stop me'.

"Turns out that was one of the worst things I could have done … your brain just needs time to heal and I wasn't giving it that so it didn't play out too nicely for me, unfortunately.

Liam Dennis says he has experienced extreme fatigue and constant headaches following a serious concussion in 2023. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

"People are catching onto it more these days. It's tricky because none of the symptoms that I have are necessarily [ones] anyone can see."

World.title: Minns staffer's legal win 'chipping away' at democracy
World.content:
In a sign of the deteriorating relationship between the Minns government and the house of parliament that keeps it in check, the premier faced an extraordinary question this week.

Would Chris Minns revive the attempts of past Labor premiers to abolish the Legislative Council？

"No," the premier said with a laugh on Thursday.

Jack Lang tried twice in the 1920s and 1930s. Bob Heffron took it to a referendum in 1961 and lost.

"Look, it's a democratic chamber. But democratic chambers are answerable to the public," Minns said.

This week, that democratic chamber voted to suspend its Labor's leader, Penny Sharpe, and censure her deputy, John Graham.

It was to protest the government's refusal to comply with the upper house's orders to produce certain documents for scrutiny.

Sharpe has been suspended from the upper house. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

But there is another reason for the tension.

A key function of the Legislative Council has been hampered after it suffered a major legal defeat to Minns's chief of staff, James Cullen.

In December, supposed powers of arrest under the Parliamentary Evidence Act 1901 were ruled invalid.

Cullen challenged the provisions to avoid being hauled before a committee examining the leaking of secret minutes.

Lovelock says the Cullen fallout "could lead to some very serious unintended consequences". (Supplied)

Since the decision, which is being appealed to the High Court, more witnesses are declining to appear at inquiries.

In March, a contractor cited the case in his refusal to attend an inquiry into a hospital plagued with safety issues.

The secretariat strongly suspects the ruling influenced three witnesses not to attend an inquiry last week into a scandal involving the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Lynn Lovelock, the clerk of the Legislative Council from 2007 to 2011, wrote the textbook on the upper house.

"What happened with the Cullen case I think has started down a path that could lead to some very serious unintended consequences in the role of what the parliament does," Lovelock told the ABC.

"What we've effectively done is taken away the right of the people to have access to information.

"This is actually chipping away at the foundations of democracy. It's affecting the people."

'This is a political chamber'

At a press conference on Wednesday, Sharpe appeared at odds with her boss over whether the parliament should have the power to force attendance.

"The fact that that's been thrown out and it's now been undermined by the court case is not great," Sharpe said.

"The situation we're in is as a result of the imprudent action of others."

Moments later, the premier confirmed that as a matter of principle he did not believe the parliament should have such powers.

"No, politicians shouldn't have the right to arrest people," Minns said.

"This is a political chamber."

Chris Minns and Penny Sharpe appeared to be at odds over parliament's power to force attendance. (ABC News)

The opposition has introduced a bill to restore the powers. It has worked with the Greens and crossbench to tack the provisions onto non-urgent pieces of legislation to send a message.

But the premier, who has previously likened a committee to a "star chamber" and "kangaroo court", made it clear he has no plans to reinstate the powers.

" I think you'd be going down a really bad route if all of a sudden [independent MLC] Mark Latham wakes up one morning and says, 'You know what? I think this dude needs to be arrested and now I have the power to do it.' "

The Parliamentary Evidence Act never gave individual MLCs the powers of arrest.

It purported to allow the president of the Legislative Council to certify a witness' non-attendance to a judge, who would then issue a warrant.

Lynn Lovelock (far left) says people can be "motivated by reasons other than upholding the powers and privileges of the parliament". (Supplied)

Lovelock said the power was never questioned before because committees were cautious about its use.

"If we feel that we're going to hit a block where somebody's going to deny our powers, we have to decide whether this is a rock we want to die on or not," she said.

"That works really well if you have reasonable people working on that. I'm not saying we have people who aren't reasonable.

"But you do have a situation where people can be motivated by reasons other than upholding the powers and privileges of the parliament.

"It can be for party political reasons. And it can be for personal reasons."

'If you've got nothing to hide you don't mind being questioned'

Among the upper house inquiries underway is a probe into claims Minns conspired to funnel illegal donations into Labor coffers a decade ago. He strenuously denies any wrongdoing.

Electoral commission reopens investigation into Minns allegations The NSW election watchdog has quietly re-opened an investigation into explosive allegations that NSW Premier Chris Minns conspired to evade state donations laws.

As the ABC reported on Thursday, the NSW Electoral Commission only reopened an investigation into the claims after a parliamentary inquiry received the allegation in November.

Greens MLC Abigail Boyd, who chairs that committee, believes Minns is worried about what her inquiry might uncover if it had the power to force attendance.

Whilst ministers in the lower house, where Minns sits, cannot be compelled to appear, their staff can.

"If you've got nothing to hide then you don't mind being questioned about things," Boyd said.

Last year she ran an inquiry into childcare exposing numerous safety failures. CEOs of providers were grilled.

The MLC doubts the bosses of those companies would have fronted the committee if hearings had been held after the Cullen decision.

Abigail Boyd believes Chris Minns is worried about what her inquiry might uncover. (Supplied)

"We were putting to them the evidence of child sexual abuse, of neglect of the most shocking, horrific things happening in the centres that they were responsible for," Boyd said.

"If you were their publicity expert, if you were their comms experts, you would be telling them, 'Whatever you do, do not go to that inquiry and answer those questions.'"

As opposition leader in 2022, Minns called for all sides of politics in the state to "place integrity at the heart" of all decisions.

"[High office] can be taken away at any time by the people and we have a duty to hand it back better than how it was when we inherited it," the Labor leader wrote in an op-ed.

But under his government, the 202-year-old parliament has become less able to shine light on things some would prefer to remain secret.

World.title: Australia is breaking its carbon bond, but there's a cost
World.content:
When carbon atoms bond with other elements, they produce compounds that can be difficult to break down. But where carbon is bound up with human lives, breakdown is difficult in different ways.

Controlled explosions at old industrial plants always attract a crowd, but if the building being demolished is a site of sentimental significance to an onlooker, the emotional response can be a little more complicated than sheer relish at the prospect of a spectacular blast.

When the big smokestack at the place where Mat and Brett Prentis had earned their living for decades was itself reduced to dust and smoke, the twin brothers felt the regret that comes with the loss of something of deep personal value.

Mat Prentis was among the workers who lost their jobs when the Port Augusta power station closed. ( )

Keen local cyclist Brett Prentis also worked at the site, which employed more than 100 people. ( )

To the east of the old plant site are powerlines and the Flinders Ranges. ( )

For more than 30 years, the 200-metre industrial obelisk had towered over three coal-fired power plants that sat at its base.

But in the aftermath of the closure of the entire operation exactly 10 years ago, chimneys were toppled.

With a wry smile, Brett likens their fate to a final "twist of the knife".

"You'd worked there for so long, and put your all into it, just to see it destroyed," he says wistfully.

"Even now, you drive [past] and you think, 'Oh, the power station's not there'," Mat adds.

"You expect to see it there — and it's not."

The falling stacks serve as a symbol of the industry they once supported.

Coal is still a very significant contributor to Australia's energy mix, but federal figures show a decline in its share — from about 75 per cent almost two decades ago to 45 per cent in 2024.

A coal train approaching the Port Augusta power station, circa early 1960s. ( )

In recent years, aging power stations across the country have been dismantled and levelled, and Australia is currently committed to a "net zero" policy to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide.

But with energy transition comes human impact, and in communities at the coalface there have already been very serious consequences.

A transmission tower in regional Australia. ( )

Bearing the brunt are such places as Victoria's Latrobe Valley and Collie in South West WA, where power stations and mines have either shut or been slated for closure.

The Ghan train passing through Port Augusta. ( )

Situated between those two regions — at the so-called "crossroads of Australia", where the nation's north-south and east-west road and rail corridors meet — is a city that might be said to serve as a warning to other towns on the cusp of decarbonisation.

End of the line

For Port Augusta, at the top of South Australia's Spencer Gulf, the date "May 9, 2016" remains a solemn one in the local annals.

It was on that day that the Northern Power Station — a significant source of employment, and a major contributor to the state's electricity output — was officially closed for a final time, leaving the workforce in limbo.

Brett remembers the gloom in the city when the closure was announced. ( )

"What am I going to do now? I'm too young to retire," local Brett Prentis can remember thinking to himself when, less than a year earlier, he first learned of the decision to shut down the plant.

During its operational life, the power station relied on coal transported by rail. ( )

About 440 workers would lose their jobs, energy company Alinta announced — almost 260 in the small outback township of Leigh Creek, where brown coal was mined and loaded onto trains destined for the power station, and 180 in Port Augusta itself.

The company had bought the plant after state energy generator ETSA was privatised in the late 1990s.

The decision to close it came as a shock to the city, and was hot on the heels of media reports suggesting the site could continue operating until at least 2030.

While Port Augusta is located on major railway lines, its old rail workshops have largely faded into memory. ( )

The Ghan passing through a crossing in Port Augusta. ( )

Railway lines pass heading the distance, and into places further afield. ( )

Despite its reputation for industry, Port Augusta has pockets of coastal beauty. ( )

The city is wedged between Spencer Gulf and the rising Flinders Ranges. ( )

Alinta CEO Jeff Dimery recounts the story of the shutdown as one involving an "intersection" of causes, including declining coal stocks in Leigh Creek and degraded infrastructure in Port Augusta.

"We were beyond the design date of the power station itself — it was one of the higher-emitting coal-fired power stations in the country," he says.

"There were issues around the reliability of the plant, given the age.

"It was off as often as it was on, and also there were some safety concerns."

Technicians work at the control panel of the Playford power station at Port Augusta. ( )

A coal tippler at the Port Augusta power station. ( )

Jeff Dimery was CEO of Alinta Energy at the time of the closure, and remains so today. ( )

The thermal power house at Port Augusta power station. ( )

Mr Dimery is adamant that prolonging its life beyond a year or two was, partly for political reasons, never a serious prospect.

"Given the stance of both federal and state governments around moving to a renewable base, there wasn't a big appetite for that," he says.

"At a federal level, there was a renewable energy target, and there was an even more aggressive renewable energy target that had been taken at a state level.

"And so, unfortunately, the very difficult decision — because we're dealing with people, livelihoods, et cetera — was made to close the plant."

Leigh Creek went from a community of about 500 in 2011 to fewer than 100 a decade later.

Port Augusta's population is around 13,000. ( )

In Port Augusta, with its population of around 13,000, the closure's effect was "traumatising" and "gut-wrenching".

Workers went elsewhere in search of jobs. ( )

"A lot of people left, a lot of operators left to go and work in other power stations," Brett Prentis says.

Rob Rozee moved from Port Augusta to Adelaide more than a decade ago. ( )

Among those who had already decided to leave was Rob Rozee.

Rob worked at the power station for decades. ( )

"It felt like Port Augusta was going to die at one stage — housing prices fell through the bloody floor. It was a really hard place to live," he says.

Rob is the father of Port Adelaide AFL captain Connor Rozee. ( )

Rob, who was employed at the plant for about 25 years, is the father of a distinguished "Power" worker of a different sort — son Connor is the captain of AFL side Port Adelaide. It was partly with an eye to his future that the Rozees reached a resolution.

Workers went in all directions trying to secure comparable jobs. ( )

By the time the plant's closure was announced, the family had gone.

Rob was a talented footballer and coach in his own right. ( )

"[The power station] used to be part of the tapestry of the town, where it was involved in the local sporting clubs," Rob says.

Rob looks back to his time in Port Augusta with deep fondness. ( )

"When private ownership took over, a lot of those things fell by the wayside. The younger generation … would look at it and think, 'Well, we're not sure that there's long-term employment prospects there'."

Promises, pipe dreams and family pain

In the wake of the power station's closure, there was a literal "power vacuum" in Port Augusta.

Locals were led to believe it would be filled by renewables.

Today, Port Augusta is surrounded by renewables projects. ( )

Wind farms, pumped hydro and grid-scale batteries were all linked to the city.

But arguably the most ambitious of the proposals — a $650 million solar thermal power plant that was tipped to create hundreds of construction jobs — never came to pass.

The failure fuelled growing cynicism and resentment, and in the area today it isn't uncommon to encounter nostalgia for the power station.

Rob Rozee has mixed feelings — he doesn't view Port Augusta's past through rose-coloured glasses, and is candid about its downsides.

An aerial view of the Playford power station in 1974, prior to the construction of the Northern station. ( )

"Port Augusta had been covered in smoke and smog for years from the power station, to the point where people had stopped drinking their tank water because of the fallout from the stack," he says.

The plant's impact on the environment was clearly visible from above. ( )

"I can remember there being big uproar and a lot of people were complaining that their cars were covered in ash."

But he also believes there wasn't enough political will to support the workforce.

"It was just easier to let the place basically disappear, or let the industry disappear and then let it fend for itself — that's how it felt for me," he says.

Model aeroplane enthusiast John Glamuzina worked at the coal-fired power station for years. ( )

Former power station worker John Glamuzina thinks the life of the plant could — and, for the community's sake, should — have been extended.

John vividly recalls the impact of the closure on locals. ( )

"The closure was different for different people — there were some who were ready to retire, and for them it was a boon and it gave them a bit of a payout," he says.

"But there were some apprentices who were just lost, they were adrift, because they were halfway through an apprenticeship and then their employer was gone."

John's home is today studded with solar panels.

But his bitter experience at the power station left him questioning some of his beliefs.

John's home is covered in rooftop solar. ( )

"I'm betwixt and between — I was on board with the whole 'save the planet' stuff, but I find myself doubting it now," he says.

"We'll know in a hundred years, maybe. Were we hoodwinked or were we really saving [it]?"

John has reflected a lot on the decision to close the plant. ( )

Those feelings aside, he counts himself as "one of the lucky ones" from the power plant.

Sundrop Farms in Port Augusta. ( )

After initially preparing to leave town with his family, he secured work at agribusiness Sundrop Farms, which uses sunlight to desalinate water for food production.

"Probably half a dozen of us from the station transferred," he says.

But other colleagues "struggled" to secure meaningful work — and in one case, the consequences were especially harrowing.

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

"The saddest thing is I lost a really good mate, Dave Kemp, to the black dog," John says.

"He moved on to a couple of other positions and was never quite happy, and eventually lost his life.

" That's by far the biggest tragedy of the transition we had to go through for the last 10 years. "

A just transition?

Within months of the plant's disconnection from the grid, an event occurred that put the closure under both a microscope and a blowtorch.

The statewide blackout of September 2016 supercharged an already fizzing debate about renewables. To an extent, the question of whether closing what had been a baseload supplier contributed to the blackout remains divisive.

Electricity projects still remain visible, and renewables dot the region. ( )

For Alinta's CEO it is "really difficult" to offer a definitive answer.

A view of a transmission tower outside Port Augusta. ( )

"Could things have been done slightly differently? Obviously, with the benefit of hindsight — and with the turn of events that occurred — the answer would be 'yes'," Mr Dimery says.

A formal review found overly sensitive protection mechanisms in wind farms were to blame for the blackout, which lasted for days in certain spots.

But even after the lights came back on, Port Augusta remained in the dark.

The city's trajectory over the following years has been sensitively but starkly captured by researchers Lisa Lumsden and Linda Connor.

Renewables advocate Lisa Lumsden was chair of the Repower Port Augusta group. ( )

University of Sydney emeritus professor Linda Connor spent time in Port Augusta tracking the impact of the closure. ( )

"It split up a lot of families; that caused a lot of stress. It was a very difficult time," Professor Connor says of the power station's closure.

The pair's paper "Energy transition in Port Augusta" presents what is in several key respects a textbook case of how not to manage sector transformation.

Among the immediate financial impacts of the closure, the paper states, was the loss of an annual payment from the power station to the city council of $500,000, an effect that led "to hikes in local council rates which snowballed into community anger".

But estimates of broader economic impact were many times that figure.

Solar and wind sites abound across the landscape. ( )

The researchers also argue that while a "renewables rush" created employment of different kinds, the jobs were well short of compensating for the work that had been lost.

"Becoming a casual worker on a construction site for a wind farm … [is] not going to replace having a long-term job as part of an important team running a massive generator," Professor Connor says.

Ms Lumsden and Professor Connor's paper was published in a book about the nation's energy transition. ( )

A term that recurs in the research is "a just transition".

Ms Lumsden defines such a transition as one in which residents — including local Indigenous communities — are "considered and accounted for and involved in the planning".

Ms Lumsden says a "just transition" is one that embraces the whole community. ( )

But the former resident of Port Augusta believes the renewables transition there was conspicuously unjust.

Ms Lumsden sometimes reflects on her time in Port Augusta. ( )

"We, maybe naively, thought that this was an incredible opportunity and we heard all the dollar signs, the amount of spend that would happen," Ms Lumsden says.

"Unfortunately, the element of justice was lost in the process of transition in South Australia."

Some places, it seems, are managing better than others.

"New South Wales is at the forefront of that — they have a system where they have legislated the requirement for community benefits at a regional level," Ms Lumsden says.

While the WA government says it has committed "nearly $700 million" for Collie's "just transition", Professor Connor also points to the east.

"The Hazelwood mine and power station closure was really a good example of a very full and involved support package from government, in cooperation with … the company itself," she says.

"[Places where] this is happening now are probably able to learn from others, and also from some very good not-for-profit organisations that are supporting the transition and working directly with communities like Collie and Gladstone."

For some locals, the aftermath of the closure created feelings of resentment. ( )

During her time in SA's north, Ms Lumsden was chair of the Repower Port Augusta group, which was pushing for a solar thermal plant.

She remains a strong advocate for renewables, but believes that social licence for them can only be paid for with meaningful support for those who potentially have most to lose from the transition — namely, local communities.

Ms Lumsden remains a strong supporter of renewables. ( )

"Our group … had high hopes for the potential of renewable energy, and unfortunately we were disappointed," she says.

"Energy transition has to happen, we do have to do it. The planet needs everyone to do it.

"[But] we just have to make sure we do it in a way that takes people along with it, and make sure that people are benefiting along the way."

Ashes to ashes, dust to dust

The land where the Port Augusta power station once stood is just south of the city.

It is a low-lying strip of mudflats and mangroves.

Loading...

To the west is the northern tip of Spencer Gulf, while in the east are national Highway One and the slopes of the Flinders Ranges.

Today, passers-by see very little evidence of the heavy machinery that once existed there.

But the power station, which possessed a forbidding grandeur that gripped the imaginations of locals, lives on in their minds like the afterglow of an industrial ghost.

"When you were a kid, you knew when you were getting home because you'd see the big chimneys, the big stacks," John Glamuzina says.

"[But now] they're all gone, knocked down. It was hard to believe at the time."

The hills around Port Augusta rise and fall. ( )

A more troubling legacy has persisted in the form of fly ash, a by-product of coal-fired combustion.

Infrastructure remains, but the station has gone. ( )

Not long after the closure, dust clouds — which were found to contain lead, barium, iron and sulphur — began blowing across town from the site, which was being stripped of its infrastructure.

Near the entrance to the old site. ( )

Even after they were demolished, the stacks cast a long shadow.

Locals enjoy quiet reflection by the waterfront. ( )

Residents have at times felt as if the plant's fate is reflected in the city itself.

A view of a Port Augusta street. ( )

"Growing up before the closure, you'd go down the main street and all the shops were just packed," says local radio presenter Dre Ngatokorua.

Radio presenter Dre Ngatokorua is a broadcaster at Umeewarra Media and an aspiring DJ. ( )

"Now, you go in and you can actually see there's not a lot of doors open.

An old "closing down" sign remains on a shopfront a decade on. ( )

"There's actually 'For Sale' signs."

When the shutdown at the power station briefly made Port Augusta the focal point of the state's attention, Dre was a teenager whose passions included playing Aussie Rules football in the local league. He couldn't help noticing the ranks had started to thin.

"All of a sudden, they're scrambling teams," he says.

"There was one team that was there when I played, and that team's not there anymore."

Dre works at Umeewarra Radio at Port Augusta. ( )

At the time of the power station closure, Dre was a teenager. ( )

Radio equipment at the station. ( )

Umeewarra Radio was established in the late 1980s. ( )

According to its website, Umeewarra promotes the "importance and relevance of Aboriginal cultures in today’s society". ( )

For Rob Rozee, the strength of the local sporting culture was one of the city's best features.

"We deliberately kept our kids in Port Augusta … [to give them a] basic upbringing in the country," he says.

As a teenager, Connor excelled at football. ( )

But sport was also one of the reasons the family eventually moved away. By the time Connor was a young adolescent, he was already showing considerable aptitude on the cricket and football fields.

"I still pinch myself every day when I turn around and I see that he's wearing the 'number one' jumper for Port Adelaide, from where he started from…," Rob says.

Rob believes country footy was a great grounding for his son. ( )

"That was never the goal when he came down here — it was just to give him opportunity and let him take that, wherever it might be.

"He still knows he's from Port Augusta and I often remind him he's got to remember where he came from and that's why he got the opportunities that he did — because he was grounded in that sort of environment."

Like a football team, Port Augusta has endured some hard knocks — but Rob believes it will keep picking itself up and dusting itself off.

He's happy to admit he sometimes misses the life there.

The region has an industrial past, but there is natural beauty everywhere. ( )

"It's always been a place," he says, "that's going to survive."

Reporting and interviews: Leah MacLennan and Daniel Keane

Port Augusta photography: Will Hunter

Video: Daniel Taylor

Video production: Sebastian Dixon

Additional ABC photography and video: Che Chorley, Brant Cumming and Kyle Harley

World.title: De Minaur's disastrous clay court form continues
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been reduced to racquet-smashing frustration as his alarming slump in form continued with another early clay-court tournament exit at the Italian Open.

Australia's world number eight was downed 4-6 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 by home favourite Matteo Arnaldi, who was cheered to the rafters at the Foro Italico by the excited Rome crowd on Friday morning.

But it was another dispiriting setback for de Minaur, who suffered his third loss in a row and had to soak up first-match defeats in back-to-back tournaments for the first time in three years.

After his opening-match drubbing to rising Rafael Jodar at the Madrid Masters, de Minaur had been expected to get a chance at revenge against the Spanish teen star in the last 32 by downing world number 106 Arnaldi.

But in another close contest after he had taken the opening set, de Minaur was the one who faltered at the end of a thrilling affair that lasted 4 minutes shy of 3 hours.

Having broken back to tie the third-set score at 4-4, de Minaur then got broken to love and was so enraged at netting a game-losing forehand that he smashed his racquet into the clay in an uncharacteristic show of disgust.

The rain that started to come down cannot have helped his mood either, as de Minaur seemed increasingly irritated by his own inconsistency. He coughed up 37 unforced errors in all, prompting him at times to shout out in exasperation towards his coaching box.

De Minaur has now lost four of his past five matches on clay, which hardly bodes well as he sets his sights on the French Open later this month.

It was not the biggest shock of the day, though, as Novak Djokovic, in his return to action after two months out with a right shoulder injury, bowed out 2-6 6-2 6-4 at the hands of a Croatian qualifier 18 years younger than him.

Novak Djokovic has suffered a shock defeat. (Getty Images: Ciancaphoto Studio/Emmanuele Ciancaglini)

The 20-year-old Dino Prižmić, world number 79 and rising, knocked out the 24-time grand slam champ with an ace on his first match point.

"He's my idol," Prižmić said.

"I just played unbelievably today."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The 38-year-old Djokovic, who had not played since losing to Jack Draper in the fourth round in Indian Wells in March, had his shoulder taped and looked far from his sharpest.

"I hope you understand I will not talk about that. I want to congratulate Dino, deservedly the winner today," Djokovic said when asked about his shoulder issue.

"I came in to have a match or more. Unfortunately, only a match. It's all right. I'm pleased at least that I fought until the end."

Alexei Popyrin remains the last Australian in the singles draw in Rome after Sydneysider Aleksandar Vukic was well beaten 6-4 6-2 by American 16th seed Tommy Paul.

AAP

World.title: Fears Deaf community will 'miss out' on news with Auslan program to end
World.content:
Australia's only daily news service delivered in Australian Sign Language will go off air next month as its federal government funding comes to an end.

Auslan90 covers the day's top stories, presented purely in Auslan by Deaf journalists, reporting on international wars, elections, cyclones, and fuel shortages.

The videos, produced by Deaf Connect, are shared on social media and have reached more than 300,000 Australians since the program launched in 2024.

Auslan90 has produced more than 400 news bulletins. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

The non-profit organisation's chief executive, Brett Casey, said the program provided the news to the Deaf community in their first language.

"A lot of Deaf people in the community, English is their second language," he told the ABC, speaking in Auslan, via an interpreter.

"They have a grasp of that second language to a varying degree."

The last show will be filmed on June 30 with funding from a grant ending.

The program has already produced more than 400 news bulletins.

Mr Casey said without the service, the Deaf community's access to news was "very limited".

Brett Casey says the program provides news to the Deaf community in their first language. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

"If you think of a hearing person … they can wake up in the morning, turn on the radio, turn on the TV and go about their daily chores while absorbing the news," he said.

"So, they have many opportunities to access that information and therefore make more informed decisions.

"But for Deaf people, the only access is one time a day that they can access news in their first language, which is Auslan."

He said Auslan90 was able to explain to the Deaf community important news stories, such as the connection between the Iran war and rising fuel prices in Australia.

"Those issues do have a significant impact on [a] person's life and ability to make an informed decision."

Understanding news clearly

Marcia Girke-Boylen, who was born deaf, said she does not miss an episode of Auslan90.

Marcia Girke-Boylen says she understands the news completely when she watches Auslan90. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

"It's so valuable," the 82-year-old told the ABC, speaking in Auslan, via an interpreter.

"My first language is Auslan, and I grew up using Auslan".

The Toowoomba resident said English subtitles on the TV were too fast to read.

"I do miss out on a lot of the words that were happening, and some of it [doesn't] make sense," Ms Girke-Boylen said.

She said the program had helped her understand the news "clearly" and gave her "100 per cent of the information".

Ms Girke-Boylen said that made her feel happy and confident.

"That's really important for the Deaf community and myself," she said.

Marcia Girke-Boylen says she watches Auslan90 bulletins each day. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

Without Auslan90, Ms Girke-Boylen said she would be "depressed".

"I will miss out on a lot of world events if it stops," she said.

" I'd be going back to those barriers again and struggling with the English and the subtitles. "

Ms Girke-Boylen said she wanted the news service extended to a full half-hour.

Government 'recognises the importance'

When the program was announced, the then social services minister, Amanda Rishworth, said the initiative would help ensure the Deaf community could access news and current affairs programs in their first language.

"Our government is committed to creating a more inclusive and accessible Australia," the Labor MP said in a 2024 media release.

Auslan interpreters missing from major updates Auslan interpreters were missing when it was declared ex-Tropical Cyclone Jasper had strengthened to a category four system, and when Gold Coast residents were urged to stay home during severe storms.

A health department spokesperson said Auslan90 had received funding through an information, linkages and capacity building (ILC) program grant to June 30.

They said grants from the ILC program would "gradually cease" as it was being replaced with a new disability peer support and connections program.

Applications for the new scheme, announced in April, are set to close in July, with successful activities due to commence in July 2027.

The spokesperson said decisions on funding were a matter for the government and were considered through established processes.

Auslan90's last show will be filmed on June 30. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

"The government recognises the importance of accessible communications, including the provision of information in Auslan," they said.

Health Minister Mark Butler was contacted for comment.

'Deaf people missing out'

Deaf Connect asked for ongoing funding for the news service in its submission ahead of the federal budget that will be handed down on May 12.

Mr Casey said there were options outside that, but he was not sure whether they would be sustainable or whether they could receive support by June 30.

Auslan90 is delivered by Deaf presenters across the country. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

He said the government funded news in other languages.

" So why again are Deaf people missing out and can't access news in their language? "

"The community have been calling out for news in their language," Mr Casey said.

The ABC News' 5pm national news bulletin on Sundays is picture-in-picture Auslan interpreted and closed-captioned.

The bulletin, which also includes a two-minute weekly news recap, can be watched weekly on ABC News Channel and ABC iview.

World.title: Victoria's treaty leaders are here and won't shy away from a challenge
World.content:
The two freshly-appointed leaders of Victoria's First Peoples' Assembly say they're ready to press on with the work of delivering the state's first ever treaty — despite a Liberal campaign to scrap the agreement.

The body will be co-led by returning assembly member and Dja Dja Wurrung traditional owner Djaran Murray-Jackson.

He will be joined by former advisor and prominent activist Meriki Onus, a first-time assembly member elected to represent the metro region.

Mr Murray-Jackson is the younger brother of former co-chair Ngarra Murray, while Onus is the sibling of Victorian former Greens turned independent senator Lidia Thorpe.

While the Assembly's recently elected members are expected to serve a four-year term, that could be cut short if the state coalition is elected in November.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson has pledged to repeal the treaty agreement, arguing it will save taxpayers nearly $1 billion over 10 years.

Djaran Murray-Jackson represents the Dja Dja Wurrung traditional owner's group, while Meriki Onus represents the Melbourne metro area. (Supplied: First Peoples' Assembly of Victoria)

The state's newest Aboriginal leaders were not shying away from the heated political contest over the future of treaty in Victoria.

"She's [Jess Wilson] just talking about all the things she wants to tear down and treaty is one of those things," Murray-Jackson said.

" I just want to hear something that she's going to build. That'd be good to hear. "

Asked about treaty's uncertain future, Meriki Onus put it simply — "Let us focus on Aboriginal affairs. Let us do our jobs".

This week, the revamped assembly held its first round of meetings on Dja Dja Wurrung country in Bendigo.

Here's how the treaty process is expected to unfold, and why it remains controversial with some Victorians.

What is treaty about?

At its core, the treaty project recognises that the land now called Victoria was home to multiple Aboriginal nations at the time of colonisation.

The First Peoples' Assembly is made up of members elected from metro and regional areas, and others appointed by traditional owner groups. (Supplied: First Peoples' Assembly of Victoria)

It also recognises that the violent dispossession of those Aboriginal communities and their exclusion from the wealth generated from their lands has caused significant intergenerational harm.

Treaty aims to give Aboriginal people greater control over government decisions, policies and funding that directly affects them, in a bid to overcome past injustices.

Victoria's treaty design, laid out in laws which passed parliament last year, has resulted in the creation of several new bodies, with different powers and functions.

All of them sit within a body named Gellung Warl, which comes from the Gunaikurnai word for "tip of the spear".

Gellung Warl is controlled by the First Peoples' Assembly. (First Peoples' Assembly of Victoria)

Under the state's treaty laws, it has the capabilities of a body corporate and is able to do things like raise revenue through commercial activities, hold shares and undertake charity work.

Like other government agencies, its actions can be scrutinised by the state's integrity watchdogs, IBAC [Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission] and the Victorian Ombudsman.

Gellung Warl isn't subject to the control or direction of the Minister for Treaty and First Peoples.

There are three distinct entities within Gellung Warl, focused on representation, truth-telling and oversight.

First Peoples' Assembly Elected by Victorian Aboriginal communities to advocate to government. Read more The First Peoples' Assembly was one of the first treaty bodies established, and is made up of 34 members. Of those, 22 are voted for in general elections open to members of Victoria's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. The other 12 are elected by the state's formally recognised traditional owner groups, who hold reserved seats. For the past few years, the assembly's work has focused on developing the systems and frameworks that are now in place as part of the treaty. From here, its role under treaty laws is to advocate for the interests of First Peoples, represent them in treaty negotiations and build capacity in the state's First Peoples, including through awarding grants from funds it controls. Nyerna Yoorrook Telkuna Tasked with helping Victorians learn about the past and the impact of colonisation. Read more Coming from the Wamba Wamba/Wemba Wemba language, Nyerna means "to sit, to listen, to hear, to remember", Yoorrook means "truth" and Tekluna means "to cure, to heal". The First Peoples' Assembly will appoint three people to Nyerna Yoorrook Telkuna, who will be tasked with promoting healing and reconciliation through a deeper understanding of colonisation and Victoria's history. How to say it: 'Nyern-ah Yoo-rrook Terl-kuun-ah' — 'ny' is with top of tongue on roof of mouth. Loading... Nginma Ngainga Wara Monitors and evaluates the state's progress in closing the gap. Read more Meaning "you will do" in the Wadi Wadi language, Nginma Ngainga Wara will consist of two or three members, appointed by the First Peoples' Assembly. Nginma Ngainga Wara is tasked with scrutinising the state government's progress in closing the gap and monitoring implementation of recommendations from the Yoorrook Justice Commission. It will also advise the First Peoples' Assembly on practical measures to improve outcomes for Indigenous communities. How to say it: Ng-in-ma Ng-ai(ay)-nga Wa-ra- 'ng' as in 'sing', 'a' as in 'car'. Loading...

How much does treaty cost?

Some critics of the treaty process have raised concerns about the cost of setting up treaty bodies such as the assembly, whose members earn roughly the same amount as backbench MPs.

This month, the opposition ramped up its attack on treaty, using costings it commissioned from the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) on the treaty process.

Those costings found the government cost of the treaty process sat at roughly $950 million over the 10 years to 2035-36.

The government has argued the PBO estimate is misleading because it includes some policies affecting Aboriginal communities, which are not necessarily specific to treaty.

Instead of treaty, a Jess Wilson-led government would establish a standalone department focused on outcomes for Indigenous Victorians, called First Nations Victoria.

The state coalition used to support Victoria's treaty plan, but leader Jess Wilson now wants to scrap the agreement if elected. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Asked about the costings of that on Friday, Ms Wilson said the opposition would reveal its costings closer to the election.

New assembly co-chair Djaran Murray-Jackson said the coalition's alternative plan had "more holes in it than Swiss cheese".

"There's no detail to it, we haven't seen a budget or what it's actually going to do," he said.

He also points to another figure produced by the Yoorrook Justice Commission's inquiry into how Victoria's colonisation has affected Aboriginal communities.

The inquiry found that from 2010 to 2023, the state of Victoria received nearly $86 billion in revenue and royalties from water, resources and land.

None of that revenue was directly distributed to traditional owners, Yoorrook found.

Does treaty change how laws are made?

Gellung Warl has no powers to veto Victorian policy or legislation.

But when members of parliament introduce new bills, they are now required to include a statement on how the bill fits with the principles of treaty and whether the First Peoples' Assembly was consulted.

The hope from treaty advocates is that with greater consultation and Aboriginal involvement in laws and policies affecting their communities, better outcomes can be achieved.

To achieve that, the treaty laws also state that the state cabinet, departmental heads and the police chief should have procedures in place allowing for briefings with the assembly twice a year.

Meriki Onus is part of the assembly for the first time. (ABC News: James Oaten)

The assembly will have the scope to determine its own priorities, with Mr Murray-Jackson promising a focus on "practical outcomes" that could be life-changing for Aboriginal Victorians.

Meriki Onus said early focus areas could include economic self-determination and monitoring progress made on changes recommended by Victoria's truth-telling inquiry, the Yoorrook Justice Commission.

"Everything that we do has to make a difference and it has to be transformative for our mob."

Will treaty close the gap on Indigenous disadvantage?

Backers of the treaty process argue that by empowering Aboriginal communities, greater progress can be made on closing the gaps in key life outcomes between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Victorians.

It's something the Nginma Ngainga Wara team will focus on monitoring under the treaty laws.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has argued funding the First Peoples' Assembly amounts to wasted bureaucracy and would not put "a single dollar into closing the gap".

Ms Wilson has said a Coalition state government would scrap treaty and manage its own consultations with the Indigenous community on improving outcomes.

Mr Murray-Jackson said he was skeptical of that plan, which sounded like "they just came up with that themselves".

"What I know, is treaty has been worked on for the past 10 years and it's a self-determined process … it's a better option," he said.

See the full list of newly elected First Peoples' Assembly members

World.title: Farrer by-election candidates walk immigration policy tightrope
World.content:
Tucked behind mirages that shimmer over endlessly flat paddocks sits the quintessentially Riverina town of Urana, in the heart of hotly contested Farrer country.

It's an unassuming grain community of about 300 residents, who were mostly born in Australia.

But despite feeling far removed from the nation's borders, immigration is vital in keeping the region's economic heart pumping.

Migrant workers are vital for some industries in the Farrer electorate. (ABC Rural: Cara Jeffery)

"I'd definitely put [immigration] up as very important because fruit pickers are relied on … so it is very important, but it has got to be a calculated decision," Urana farmer, businessman and local councillor Patrick Bourke said.

But finessing that "calculated" policy to fit Farrer is complicated, as candidates in today's by-election have discovered.

Key Farrer industries like health, manufacturing, hospitality and agriculture would be jeopardised without migrant labour.

Urana-based nurse Carol Kirkby said immigration was vital for regional towns like hers.

The town of Urana lies in the heart of Farrer. (Supplied: Urana Shire Council)

"There would often be no staff in aged care facilities, we would be short-staffed in health care facilities, we just wouldn't be able to function," she said.

But some voters also worry that immigration strains housing and healthcare.

Mr Bourke saw first-hand while serving as Federation Council mayor in 2024 how those worries were preyed upon when neo-Nazis descended on Corowa, where multinational meat processor JBS is based.

A group of Neo-Nazis staged a rally in Corowa, NSW, in 2024. (Supplied: Kendra Smith)

"There is no room for that," Mr Bourke said.

"That's not what Australia stands for or should be or should put up with."

'Who else will do the work?'

Pita Foliaki Lokotui works as a country liaison officer for Vanuatu Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme workers and speaks regularly with people across the electorate about welfare issues they are facing.

A sign on the outskirts of Leeton in Farrer declares the regional town is welcoming to migrants. (ABC News: Doug Dingwall)

He says nearly 7,000 Vanuatuan people, or Ni-Vans, work in the PALM scheme, with 90 per cent in horticulture.

"I don't doubt that migration has its challenges, [but] to me, the PALM scheme is needed, [and] if they stop that, then who else will do the work?" he said.

Mr Foliaki Lokotui said that reducing the number of Vanuatu workers would only slow the horticulture industry, and since the PALM scheme required farmers to provide housing, access to housing would become an issue only if a worker decided to live in the region permanently.

The PALM scheme was introduced to fill jobs in industries such as agriculture, meat processing and aged care. (ABC News: Lucy Cooper)

However, he said other challenges existed, such as occasional workplace cultural clashes.

"There are farmers who are receptive to the culture, there are others who focus on running a business and are not receptive to the culture, which is fine," he said.

"If there's a farmer that's being racist, there are things in place to sort of help the farmer understand … if you want the business, then you have to sort of look at things differently.

"But if not, then we're going to go down the process to remove the workers and send them elsewhere."

Flip-flop over Farrer immigration

Australia's net overseas migration for the 2024-25 financial year was 306,000, down from 429,000 a year earlier, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

It included 88,000 permanent visa holders, 157,000 international students, 78,000 working holiday makers, and 46,000 temporary skilled workers.

One Nation, which could clinch Farrer at today's by-election, has long called Australia's immigration system "broken", pledging to cap annual arrivals at 130,000.

Farrer's One Nation candidate, David Farley, has built a successful career in Australian cotton, which relies heavily on temporary visa holders to meet seasonal labour needs, and has inadvertently highlighted the policy tightrope facing some candidates in the seat.

One Nation candidate for Farrer David Farley, centre, at an election forum. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

At a Charles Sturt University election forum last week, Mr Farley said immigration should match housing, health and education needs and that the 306,000 net migration figure may not be enough.

"Is 306,000 too many? No, it's probably not," he said.

"If we're successful in One Nation's water policies, we're going to need more labour, and we're going to need more [skilled] labour quickly."

The next day, Mr Farley wrote on social media that 306,000 was too many amid a housing crisis.

"One Nation will cap immigration at 130,000 per year," he wrote.

"We need to catch up on housing, services, water and infrastructure for Australians already living here."

He told the ABC on the eve of the by-election that skilled migrant programs like the PALM scheme were working, but "bench sitters" who did not contribute were not welcome.

The Liberals, Nationals, One Nation and an independent are among those contesting the Farrer by-election. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

Independent Michelle Milthorpe has outlined that regional economies need migrants to sustain industries, but also need housing and services to support newcomers.

She wants regional communities to be in charge of driving migration pathways.

Her policy includes aligning skilled worker visas with local demand rather than a national list, establishing regional multicultural centres, and fast-tracking housing projects.

The by-election falls just weeks after the Coalition announced the first instalment of its Australian Values Migration Plan, after long-advocating for lower migration levels.

The Coalition has also announced it will link overseas migration to housing supply as part of its migration strategy.

World.title: Depth of antisemitism exposed by anonymous witnesses before commission
World.content:
Her name and face concealed for protection, a 13-year-old girl told a royal commission on antisemitism she no longer felt safe being Jewish in Australia.

The teenager has so far been the youngest person to give evidence at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which was announced in the wake of the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.

Fifteen people were killed during the shooting at a Hanukkah celebration by the beach on December 14.

The royal commission is examining the circumstances of the incident and the spread of antisemitism in Australia that preceded it.

Witnesses have included a relative of someone killed in the shooting, Holocaust survivors and health workers affected by antisemitism in the workplace.

The royal commission is looking at the spread of antisemitism in Australia. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

A large number used pseudonyms to protect their identity and safety.

As a further protection, the anonymous girl addressed the commission through a voice recording which was not formally tabled to the inquiry.

'Worried to be a Jewish kid'

Her young voice was heard over the commission live stream on Wednesday, recounting how she was at a bat mitzvah party at Bondi Pavillion when the celebration was locked down due to the shooting.

She did not hear the gunfire but watched hundreds running from the scene at nearby Archer Park.

"I still don't like to see the [pedestrian] bridge when go to Bondi," the girl said.

" It makes me feel worried to be a Jewish kid in Australia. "

She said she has friends who jump at the sound of a balloon popping and avoid playing laser tag in the wake of the attack.

"A lot of my friends are now scared to have a sleepover or go on school camp because they don't want to be away from their parents and are worried something bad might happen again."

Fifteen people were killed during the December 14 terrorist attack at Bondi Beach. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

The girl said her father wanted to enrol her in self-defence classes after the terror attack in "case anyone tries to hurt me because I am Jewish".

"I don't think Jewish kids should be scared to live normally like other kids do, it's not fair," she said.

Almost all witnesses told the commission they noticed a marked increase in antisemitic incidents and rhetoric after October 7, 2023 where 1,200 people were killed when Hamas attacked Israel.

Military and civilian hostages were also taken back to Gaza, and Israel subsequently declared war with Hamas.

After this, parents said they noticed how antisemitism had affected the lives of their children in a way they had not experienced during their own Australian childhoods.

Racism, bullying part of school life

One of the most serious cases heard by the commission involved a 13-year-old boy being bullied at his Darwin public school after he started wearing a Star of David necklace following a family trip to Israel.

His father, the son of a Holocaust survivor, told the commission the bullying started in the form of slurs and offensive gestures before escalating to physical abuse.

"The physical bullying included him being squeezed until he couldn't breathe … being dragged across the floor to the point he received a carpet burn to his upper arm and being thrown into the garbage bin," he told the commission.

Parents told the commission they noticed how antisemitism had affected the lives of their children. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The father, who remained anonymous for the hearing, said the teenager's anxiety increased after the bullying and he refused to go to school.

He said the school "did nothing" to address the family's concerns.

"I mentioned that my son was experiencing racism and physical bullying. It took 10 days for the vice principal to come back to me with the results of his investigation," he said.

The family has now relocated to regional New South Wales and the teenager started at his new school earlier this year.

The father told the commission he discovered just this week that his son was experiencing antisemitic bullying again, and had been soon after he started school.

"Even though I checked in on him, he just couldn't bring himself to bring it up because he just was hoping it would go away," he said.

'I don't know how the genie goes back in'

The commission also heard from a former crisis support call centre volunteer whose nephew died during the Bondi terror attack.

She said she stopped volunteering after the Hamas attacks, due to an increasing number of callers making antisemitic comments.

She said she assessed the callers were not having genuine mental health crises and instead "wanted to offload".

The anonymous witness said her family received much support after the Bondi shooting, and said there were some in the community who understood the impact of antisemitism on Jewish Australians.

Man wears swastika shirt outside antisemitism royal commission A man wearing a T-shirt with a swastika was initially moved on by police outside the royal commission into antisemitism in Sydney, before later being arrested.

"I think it is a section of our society that is ruining it, and I don't know how the genie goes back in," she said.

The proceedings in Sydney have been heavily policed, with one man seen outside the building wearing a swastika shirt subsequently charged.

One witness given the pseudonym Benjamin F said he had been anxious he would be confronted by similar "hecklers" while addressing the commission.

He gave evidence on another theme that emerged over the week: how members of the Jewish community felt they had been exiled from groups which claimed to be progressive and inclusive.

Exclusion form once-safe spaces

Benjamin F described his conversion from Roman Catholicism to Judaism as a "second coming out" and was subject to a "profound" level of hate.

"It was quite horrific actually," he said.

" Those spaces I once considered safe, I once considered my community, I would not question going to a gay bar or club … that has changed significantly. "

Benjamin F spoke of feeling a "guttural" fear for his life as he prepared to march with Jewish LGBTQIA+ group Dayenu at Sydney's Mardi Gras parade earlier this year.

'Scared for my life': Jewish teacher feared Mardi Gras attack He told the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion he was embraced by the LGBTQIA+ community when he came out as gay as a teenager, but the experience was markedly different when he told loved ones of his religious conversion.

Before the march, the Pride in Protest group had been banned from the event over offensive comments about Dayenu.

"Once we were walking up Oxford Street … it was probably one of the scariest moments of my life," Benjamin F said.

Public hearings are continuing, with more than 9,600 people making submissions to the commission.

Some sessions are expected to be conducted behind closed doors to avoid prejudice to national security and ongoing criminal proceedings.

World.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to three-day ceasefire, says Trump
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russia, Ukraine agree to three-day ceasefire, says Trump Updated May 9, 2026 — 7:30am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump said there will be a three-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, as well as a prisoner swap. The ceasefire, which Trump said would run from May 9 to May 11, coincides with Russia’s Victory Day celebrations, the US president said in a social media post on Friday. US President Donald Trump during a Mother’s Day luncheon at the White House on Friday. Bloomberg Trump said that Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have both agreed to the proposal. “This Ceasefire will include a suspension of all kinetic activity, and also a prison swap of 1,000 prisoners from each Country,” Trump wrote. “Hopefully, it is the beginning of the end of a very long, deadly, and hard fought War,” he wrote on Truth Social.



Trump’s announcement also said each country, locked in more than four years of conflict, would be exchanging 1000 prisoners of war. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Disintegration’: Trump angers Europe with tariffs and troop withdrawal Both Kyiv and Moscow have accused the other of violating ceasefires declared separately this week as Russia readies to hold a Victory Day parade on May 9 that marks the 1945 Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated by the lack of progress in ending the Ukraine-Russia war, and a halt in fighting offers a bit of good news for the US president, whose war against Iran with Israel has hurt his domestic approval rating. Efforts to end the Iran war, now in its third month, appeared stalled amid new flare-ups in fighting in the Gulf. Zelensky, writing on Telegram, confirmed the ceasefire had been arranged as part of US negotiating efforts and that humanitarian issues remained a key priority.



“That is why today, within the framework of the negotiation process mediated by the American side, we received Russia’s agreement to conduct a prisoner of war exchange in the format of 1000 for 1000,” Zelensky wrote. Zelensky also issued a tongue-in-cheek decree “allowing” Russia’s May 9 military parade to proceed and saying Ukrainian weapons would not target Red Square. Officials said on Thursday that Ukraine’s top ​negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had arrived in Miami for a series of meetings with US ‌representatives as peace talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine have stalled in recent months. The US-brokered talks ⁠are deadlocked over Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. Moscow demands Kyiv pull troops back from parts ​of the region it has failed to capture in its four-year full-scale invasion. Ukraine says it ​will not cede land that it controls. Moscow and Kyiv have both accused each other of violating ceasefires that each has separately declared.
